did_you_know.text: Did you know? Daniel begins the chapter during the first year of the reign of Darius son of Ahasuerus, who is called here a Mede and is said to have ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans.
Did you know? Daniel says that he studied the “books” in order to understand Jeremiah’s prophecy about the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation.
Did you know? Daniel’s response to understanding the prophecy is prayer, supplication, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes—expressions of humility and mourning.

Did you know? In his confession, Daniel uses several terms for sin: “we have sinned,” “we have acted wickedly,” “we have done wrong,” and “we have rebelled,” emphasizing the seriousness of the people’s turning away from the LORD’s commandments.

Did you know? Daniel presents a clear contrast: “Righteousness belongs to you, LORD,” while the people have “shame on our faces.” In his prayer, he includes both Judah and Jerusalem, as well as the Israelites who were exiled to various countries.

Did you know? Daniel connects the national disaster with the words of the Law and the prophets, noting that the great calamity that came upon Jerusalem occurred in accordance with the warnings given beforehand.
Did you know? Daniel emphasizes that his plea does not rest on the righteousness of the people, but on the LORD’s abundant mercy.
Did you know? While Daniel is praying, Gabriel—whom he had also seen in an earlier vision—comes to him at the time of the evening offering.

Did you know? Gabriel says that seventy “weeks” have been decreed for the people of Israel and for Jerusalem, including the end of transgression, atonement for sin, the bringing in of everlasting righteousness, and the sealing up of vision and prophecy.

Did you know? The vision of the seventy weeks divides the period mentioned into units of seven weeks, sixty-two weeks, and one week; the text also describes rebuilding, distress, destruction, and the cessation of sacrifice and offering.
